This is a commonly-discussed question, and the general consensus is strongly in favor of loading them if you wish. The springs are not harmed by prolonged compression. (Oddly enough, what does wear them out is cycling between being compressed and uncompressed, but it takes awhile, and they are cheap and easy to replace as needed).

The one exception to this rule is antique guns, with old funky springs. Leaving the spring relaxed on your 100 year old SAA is probably a good idea.

One a related note, this same rule applies to leaving the action open - you won't harm the springs by storing your empty rifle with the bolt locked back. This is good practice for a couple of reasons; first, we always open the action the moment we pick them up anyway, and second, it eliminates the entirely unnecessary step of closing the action and pulling the trigger before storage, that so many people routinely do. Every now and again somebody blows a hole through the floor, and there's just no reason for any of it.

Pistols too. Unless they are antiques with weird springs, or left loaded and ready on purpose, store them with the action locked back.

How to keep your mags working:

Don’t overload them. It is apparently quite common for dummies to load 31 rounds into polymer mags designed for 30 rounds. This can stress the feedlips and be the beginnings of a fracture point

Use anti-tilt followers. Especially relevant if using older USGI magazines for an AR. You can pick up packs of upgraded followers for cheap.

Make sure the feedlips are in spec. For polymer, check for cracks or visible bowing. For metal lips look for bends or chips. Do not try to rebend a metal lip back into spec, you won’t be able to eyeball it and it will weaken the metal even more. Salvage internals and toss bad mags.

If the mag has been loaded and carried for a long time, such as a patrol officer’s magazine or a soldier on a deployment, it should be periodically emptied and cleaned. This is nothing to do with spring compression, but to ensure the inside is not dirty from the environment.
